config.title: Vintage Shopping in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: Straight answers on where to find second-hand and vintage in Berlin, how the kilo shops work, and why Sunday is the one day the plan falls apart.

items.q: Where is the best vintage shopping in Berlin?
items.a: For a first visit, **Neukolln around Weserstrasse** is the single best area: the densest cluster of small, hand-picked shops, all walkable. **Friedrichshain around Boxhagener Platz** is the budget end with big second-hand halls. **Kreuzberg on Bergmannstrasse** is worth it mainly for the pay-by-weight kilo store. **Mitte** is the most central and the most upscale, and **Prenzlauer Berg** is polished with the Mauerpark flea market next door. Pick one district and shop it on foot rather than chasing shops across the city.

items.q: Is vintage shopping in Berlin cheap?
items.a: Less than its reputation suggests. Berlin used to be a bargain city for second-hand, but prices have climbed and the scene has moved toward curated, boutique-priced shops. You can still find good value at the big halls like Humana and at the kilo stores, but genuinely cheap everyday vintage is harder to find than it was. Treat it as quality hunting, not bargain hunting.

items.q: How do the pay-by-weight kilo shops work?
items.a: You do not pay per garment. Clothes are grouped by coloured tags, each colour has a fixed price per kilo, and everything you pick is weighed together at the till. Rates run roughly from the low twenties to near a hundred euro a kilo depending on the tag, so light items like shirts and dresses are the real value while a heavy coat can cost as much as a small pile. **Colours** on Bergmannstrasse in Kreuzberg and **Made in Berlin** in Mitte are the best known, and both usually discount the kilo price on a Tuesday.

items.q: Are Berlin vintage shops open on Sunday?
items.a: No. Under Berlin's shop-closing law, almost all clothing shops, including vintage and second-hand, are **closed on Sundays**. If you have only a Sunday, the second-hand option is the flea markets, which run Sunday only: **Mauerpark** in Prenzlauer Berg from mid-morning, plus **Boxhagener Platz** in Friedrichshain and Arkonaplatz. Save the shops themselves for Monday to Saturday.

items.q: Do I need cash, or do the shops take cards?
items.a: The big chains, Humana, Colours and Made in Berlin, take cards. But the small owner-run shops in Neukolln and Kreuzberg often prefer cash and a few set a card minimum, so it is worth carrying some notes for a day of browsing the independents.

items.q: What is the most central area for second-hand shopping?
items.a: **Mitte**, around Mulackstrasse and Neue Schonhauser Strasse in the old fashion quarter. It is the priciest cluster and best for designer resale, but it is the easiest to combine with sightseeing. My free walking tour ends at Hackescher Markt, a two-minute walk away, so it is simple to browse there after the tour.

items.q: When do the vintage shops open?
items.a: The big halls like Humana open around 10:00 and run to about 20:00, Monday to Saturday. The small independent shops tend to open later, often 11:00 or 12:00, and some close one weekday, so for the tiny owner-run places it is worth a quick check of the current listing before you set out.
